CHAPTER 8: MARKET STRUCTURES

INTRODUCTION
- Market: a place where goods and services are bought and sold; where buyers and sellers interact.
- Factors that distinguish markets (Table 8.1): number of sellers; barriers to entry/exit; type of good (perfect substitutes or slightly different); product differentiation (competitive or generic advertising); whether firms are independent or interdependent.
- Four market structures, from fewest to most sellers: monopoly (one firm), oligopoly (small number of large interdependent firms), imperfect/monopolistic competition (many independent sellers of differentiated products), perfect competition (thousands of sellers of identical products).
- Examples: monopoly - only cinema in a small town, school canteen, Irish Rail. Oligopoly - Irish retail banking (AIB, BOI, Permanent TSB, KBC), European chocolate (Nestle, Cadbury, Mars), mobile networks (Vodafone, Three, Eir). Monopolistic - artisan foods, fast-food outlets, coffee shops in a city. Perfect competition - agricultural produce, e.g. US wheat.

KEY TERMS
- Equilibrium position: firms produce where MR = MC (and MC cuts MR from below) - the profit-maximising condition. This then shows the price, the profit and the cost per unit (efficiency).
- Normal profit: earned when AR = AC; the minimum profit needed to stay in business in the long run.
- Abnormal (supernormal) profit: earned when AR > AC; profit above normal profit. SNPs can attract new firms if there are no barriers to entry, eliminating them in the long run.
- High market concentration: a small number of large sellers dominate (e.g. mobile networks, banks, insurers). Bad for consumers - less choice, higher prices; firms have market power over price.
- Low market concentration: many smaller sellers (e.g. fruit market, city restaurants). Good for consumers - more choice, lower prices; in perfect competition firms have no control over price.
- Four-firm concentration ratio: add the percentage market shares of the four largest firms (e.g. 80% = high concentration).
- Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI): square each firm's percentage market share and add the results. Value between 1 and 10,000.
- HHI spectrum: 1 to 1,500 low concentration; 1,500 to 2,500 moderate; 2,500 to 10,000 high. Closer to 1 = more competitive. 10,000 = pure monopoly (100 squared).
- Short run: at least one factor of production fixed. Long run: all factors can be varied.

PERFECT COMPETITION - CHARACTERISTICS
- Exists more in theory than reality; some agricultural markets come close, e.g. Moore Street in Dublin (fruit, veg, flower sellers selling identical products).
- 1. Freedom of entry/exit - no barriers. Barriers to entry/exit: factors that prevent new firms entering or leaving a market, e.g. needing a permit.
- 2. Homogenous (identical) goods; perfect substitutes widely available; no product differentiation or competitive advertising.
- 3. Many buyers - each buys a tiny share, so cannot influence price.
- 4. High degree of knowledge - sellers know profit levels; buyers know price and quality, so a seller charging above the market price has no customers.
- 5. Many sellers who are price takers - each sells a tiny share so price is set by the market.
- 6. Firms aim to maximise profit (MR = MC).

PRICE DETERMINATION AND THE FIRM'S DEMAND CURVE
- Banana example (Table 8.5): price/QD/QS - 0.20: 10,000/2,000; 0.40: 8,000/4,000; 0.60: 6,000/6,000; 0.80: 4,000/8,000; 1.00: 2,000/10,000. Market price = 60c.
- Figure 8.2 (in words): left - market demand and supply crossing at 60c; right - the individual firm's horizontal demand line at 60c labelled D/MR/AR.
- The firm's demand curve is horizontal: demand is perfectly elastic - any price rise means demand falls to zero.
- Table 8.6: at 60c, TR for 1 to 5 units = 60c, 1.20, 1.80, 2.40, 3.00 euro; MR and AR always 60c.
- MR = change in TR / change in Q = P. AR = TR / Q = P. So in perfect competition P = MR = AR.

PERFECT COMPETITION - SHORT RUN EQUILIBRIUM (FIGURE 8.3)
- Diagram in words: horizontal D/MR/AR at P1; U-shaped AC; Nike-shaped MC cutting MR from below at E above Q1; AC at Q1 is point C (value C1), below P1.
- Quantity: Q1, where MR = MC (point E).
- Price: P1, set by the market (price taker).
- Costs: C, not the lowest point on AC - inefficient.
- Profits: AR > AC so supernormal profits; area P1C1CE.

PERFECT COMPETITION - LONG RUN EQUILIBRIUM (FIGURES 8.4 AND 8.5)
- Knowledge of SNPs and no barriers to entry mean new sellers enter.
- Market supply shifts right; market price falls from P(old) to P(new); the firm's demand curve moves down.
- Long run: firm produces Q2 (lower) at price P2 (lower), where MR = MC at E.
- E is at the lowest point of AC - the firm is efficient. AR = AC so normal profit.
- Diagram in words: the new D/MR/AR line is tangent to the bottom of the AC curve, and MC passes through that point.

PERFECT COMPETITION - WORKED EXAMPLES
- Price 10 euro, Q = 100, AC = 8 euro: MR = AR = 10 euro; TR = 1,000 euro; TC = 800 euro.
- AR 60 euro, AC 45 euro, Q 100: MR = P = 60 euro; TR = 6,000 euro; TC = AC x Q = 4,500 euro; SNP = 1,500 euro (or 15 euro x 100).
- HHI: 10,000 wheat farmers each with 0.01%: 0.01 squared x 10,000 = 1 (opposite end to monopoly).
- HHI: 77 apple sellers - 70 with 1%, 5 with 2%, 2 with 10%: 70 + 20 + 200 = 290, low concentration, highly competitive but not 'perfect'.

ADVERTISING
- Competitive advertising: promotes one firm's goods over competitors' (banks, insurers, mobile networks, drinks companies, toothpaste makers).
- Generic advertising: promotes the output of a whole industry without naming suppliers (National Dairy Council, An Bord Bia - dairy, lamb, pork, beef).
- Generic advertising is common in perfect competition. Competitive advertising does not occur because: buyers already have full knowledge of price and quality; products are identical so a firm would advertise rivals' output too but pay all the cost; it would raise costs, so the firm would not be maximising profit.

EVALUATION OF PERFECT COMPETITION
- Advantages: many sellers to choose from (English Market in Cork, Moore Street); lower prices than monopoly and only normal profit in the long run, so no exploitation; higher total market output; efficient in the long run (lowest point on AC; no wasteful competitive advertising).
- Disadvantages: no incentive to innovate or invest in R&D (rivals copy); lack of variety (homogenous goods); no firm can expand to gain economies of scale; normal profit only, so firms can be close to going out of business (farmers say beef and milk prices barely cover costs).

SUPPLY CURVES OF A PERFECTLY COMPETITIVE FIRM
- Short run: the firm must at least cover AVC (e.g. labour and raw materials per unit). At prices P1, P2, P3 it supplies Q1, Q2, Q3 where MR = MC; below P3 (minimum AVC) it stops. Short run supply curve = the part of MC above AVC.
- Long run: the firm must cover ATC (AVC + AFC such as rent, loan repayments, insurance). Long run supply curve = the part of MC above AC (ATC).

MONOPOLY - DEFINITION AND CHARACTERISTICS
- Monopoly: only one supplier, no close substitute, protected by barriers to entry.
- Pure monopoly: one firm has 100% of the market. A dominant firm has significant monopoly power, e.g. Google had 96% of the Irish search engine market in 2020 ('near monopoly').
- 1. One seller - the firm is the industry, e.g. An Post (universal postal service).
- 2. Aims to maximise profit (MR = MC, MC cutting from below).
- 3. Faces a downward-sloping demand curve (Law of Demand). It can set price OR quantity, but not both.
- 4. Barriers to entry exist - the source of monopoly power.

BARRIERS TO ENTRY
- Patents: give the inventor the sole right to supply the invention for a period; reward R&D (e.g. pharmaceutical drugs).
- Copyright: gives creators of books, music, poems, films, artwork the exclusive right to reproduce their work.
- High/prohibitive start-up costs: e.g. a new train operator competing with Irish Rail would need to buy trains.
- Economies of scale: a large airline with thousands of flights has lower cost per passenger than a new small airline; new entrants take years to gain these.
- Sole access to raw materials: De Beers controlled diamond mines from the late 1800s into the 20th century.
- Statutory/legal monopoly: a law gives one firm (often state-owned) a single licence, e.g. Dublin Bus until 2017, when 10% of routes were privatised and awarded to Go-Ahead.

MONOPOLY REVENUE CURVES (TABLE 8.12)
- Price/Q/TR/MR/AR: 20/1/20/20/20; 18/2/36/16/18; 16/3/48/12/16; 14/4/56/8/14; 12/5/60/4/12 (euro).
- AR = price, so the demand curve is the AR curve.
- MR lies below AR and diverges from it because to sell more the firm must cut the price on ALL units, not just the extra one.
- Diagram in words (Figure 8.10): downward-sloping D/AR line; steeper MR line below it starting at the same point.

MONOPOLY EQUILIBRIUM (FIGURE 8.11)
- Diagram in words: downward D/AR, steeper MR below it, U-shaped AC, MC cutting MR from below at E. Up from Q1 to D/AR at X gives P1; up to AC at C gives C1.
- Quantity Q1 (MR = MC). Price P1 (read off demand curve at X).
- Costs: C, not lowest point on AC - inefficient.
- Profits: AR > AC, supernormal profits in short AND long run because barriers stop entry. Area P1C1CX.
- Worked example: AR 20 euro, AC 10 euro, 8 units. Price 20 euro; TC 80 euro; SNP = 160 - 80 = 80 euro (or 8 x 10).

EVALUATION OF MONOPOLY
- Market failure: inefficiency in the allocation of goods and services in a free market. Monopoly power to restrict output and keep prices high is an example.
- Advantages: economies of scale (lower cost per unit); capital for R&D (e.g. Facebook improving its platforms); job security for employees; state monopolies provide loss-making essential services (e.g. Irish Rail's Limerick-Ballybrophy line); non-duplication of services (no parallel rail lines).
- Disadvantages: inefficient (not at lowest AC); little incentive to innovate, poor service; higher prices and restricted output - exploitation; taxpayers must fund regulators; loss-making state monopolies need subsidies (2016: 550 euro per passenger on Limerick-Ballybrophy).

HHI AND MERGERS - AIRLINE EXAMPLE
- Airlines A 40%, B 42%, C 8%, D 10%. Before merger HHI = 1,600 + 1,764 + 64 + 100 = 3,528 (already high).
- If A and B merge (82%): 6,724 + 64 + 100 = 6,888. Regulators would probably refuse - one dominant firm, likely a monopoly on some routes.
- European Commission: post-merger HHI over 2,000 suggests a concentrated market and competition concern. Irish CCPC: over 1,000 concentrated; over 2,000 highly concentrated.

REGULATION AND DEREGULATION
- Regulators stop monopolies charging excessive prices, restricting output, providing poor quality, ignoring health and safety; they protect taxpayers from losses of state monopolies.
- Regulators deal with complaints, approve/reject price increases, carry out inspections and bring prosecutions. They can block mergers/takeovers, e.g. Ryanair was prevented from taking over Aer Lingus.
- Deregulation: removing regulations/laws that prevent new firms entering a market. Since the 1990s in Ireland, e.g. electricity - ESB (Electric Ireland) lost its monopoly; Energia, SSE Airtricity, Pinergy, Bord Gais Energy entered.
- Effects: more choice, lower prices (switching discounts), state firm becomes more efficient, new jobs; but possible job losses in an inefficient former monopoly that over-hired.

PRICE DISCRIMINATION
- Consumer surplus: the difference between what a consumer pays and what they would be willing to pay rather than do without.
- Price discrimination: charging different customers different prices for the same good/service, where the difference is not due to differences in costs of production.
- First degree: least common; one-to-one confidential services; each consumer pays their maximum price, removing all consumer surplus (solicitor, medical consultant).
- Second degree: bulk discounts, e.g. one bar for 1 euro vs three bars for 2 euro; based on the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility.
- Third degree: most common; groups charged differently, e.g. hairdresser or bus company charging students and pensioners less. The lower-price group has relatively elastic demand; others have relatively inelastic demand. Extracts some, not all, consumer surplus.
- Conditions: 1. Some monopoly power (barriers stop rivals competing away profits). 2. Able to identify groups with different price elasticities (third degree). 3. Markets kept separate - no reselling; so more common in services (a haircut or legal advice cannot be resold). 4. Consumer indifference - high-price customers do not mind.

MONOPOLISTIC (IMPERFECT) COMPETITION - CHARACTERISTICS
- Shows elements of both monopoly and perfect competition. Examples: coffee shops, restaurants, hairdressers. Do not confuse 'monopoly' and 'monopolistic'.
- 1. No barriers to entry/exit (e.g. no licence needed). 2. Many buyers - none can influence price. 3. Many independent sellers who set their own price; downward-sloping demand. 4. Close substitutes, so demand is more elastic (flatter) than a monopolist's. 5. Knowledge of profits - SNPs attract entrants. 6. Profit maximisation (MR = MC). 7. Product differentiation - similar but not identical products; branding, competitive advertising, packaging, quality, innovation, loyalty cards, customer service.
- Brand loyalty: the tendency of some customers to keep buying a certain brand rather than competing brands.
- Successful differentiation/brand loyalty = steeper demand curve (relatively inelastic), more power over price. Less successful = flatter demand curve (relatively elastic), less power over price.
- AR and MR relationship same as monopoly.

MONOPOLISTIC COMPETITION - EQUILIBRIUM
- Short run (Figure 8.13): like monopoly but slightly flatter demand. Q1 where MR = MC; price P1; cost C not at lowest AC - inefficient; AR > AC so SNPs (area P1C1CX).
- Long run: SNPs plus knowledge and no barriers attract new firms; the firm's D/AR and MR shift down to the left (Figure 8.14).
- Long run (Figure 8.15): Q2 lower than Q1, P2 lower than P1; still not at lowest AC - inefficient; AR = AC so normal profit. Diagram in words: D/AR curve just touches (is tangent to) the AC curve at the price P2, to the left of AC's lowest point.
- Worked examples: long run Q = 30, P = AR = AC = 20 euro, TR = 600 euro. AR 15 euro, Q 10: P 15, TR 150, AC 15, TC 150 euro.

EVALUATION OF MONOPOLISTIC COMPETITION
- Advantages: wide choice of firms; wide variety and innovation (changing menus, many coffee variations); jobs in marketing and advertising; loyalty rewards; lower prices than monopoly; normal profit in the long run so no exploitation.
- Disadvantages: inefficient in the long run - resources spent on advertising, marketing and brand loyalty instead of output; higher prices and lower output than perfect competition.

FOUR-FIRM RATIO GUIDE (TABLE 8.17)
- 1-50% low concentration (monopolistic in middle to upper end); 50-80% medium (generally oligopolistic); 80-100% high (significant market power). Four similar firms over 80% = highly concentrated oligopoly.
- Fast-food example: 20 restaurants - one 8%, six 6%, seven 5%, five 4%, one 1%. Four-firm ratio = 8 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 26% (low, monopolistic). HHI = 64 + 216 + 175 + 80 + 1 = 536 (low).

OLIGOPOLY - FEATURES
- Firms are interdependent: they take likely reactions of rivals into account, especially on price.
- 1. High concentration ratio - examples: EU chocolate (Cadbury, Mars, Nestle); Irish retail banks (BOI, AIB, PTSB, EBS, KBC); telecoms (Vodafone, Three, Eir); health insurance (VHI, Irish Life Health, Laya, Aviva); groceries (SuperValu, Lidl, Aldi, Dunnes, Tesco, Spar).
- 2. Product differentiation - close substitutes; heavy advertising and sponsorship (bank slogans: 'Never Stop Competing' BOI, 'We Back Brave' AIB, 'Doing Different' KBC); brand loyalty and loyalty cards.
- 3. Interdependence leading to price rigidity - e.g. similar mortgage rates across lenders.
- Price rigidity: prices tend not to change even if costs change; a rise loses sales to rivals who do not follow, a cut is matched by rivals (price war).
- Price constancy (different): leaving price unchanged because changing it costs more (reprinting menus or catalogues, changing adverts).
- 4. Barriers to entry: economies of scale; high start-up costs (hundreds of millions to compete with Nestle, Mars, Cadbury); limit pricing; brand loyalty (reluctance to switch banks or health insurer); brand proliferation.
- Limit pricing: existing firms charge lower prices than they could to make entry unprofitable and deter new firms (e.g. airlines cutting fares on a new entrant's routes). Illegal.
- Brand proliferation: one firm offers many variations of the same good, e.g. Coca-Cola's range of drinks.
- 5. Non-price competition (to avoid price wars): advertising/sponsorship; loyalty cards; free gifts and special offers (Sky VIP, 3Plus); quality of service (broadband speeds).
- 6. Aims other than profit maximisation: avoid regulation (2019 insurance scrutiny over public liability prices); avoid extra taxes (main banks pay no corporation tax due to the financial crisis); discourage entrants (limit pricing); become market leader (Revolut, founded 2015, had 1.2 million Irish customers by 2021 by charging very low fees).
- 7. Collusion - cartel: two or more competitors agree not to compete to raise profits at consumers' expense; usually illegal. Can be implicit (informal) or explicit (formal).

FORMS OF COLLUSION
- Limit pricing.
- Price fixing: agreeing not to sell below a price or fixing discounts. BA and Virgin Atlantic fixed fuel surcharges; Virgin got immunity for reporting it; BA was heavily fined.
- Price leadership: the dominant firm sets the price and others follow.
- Restricting output: OPEC (1960, 13 oil-exporting nations, about 40% of world oil supply) formally agrees output to influence world oil prices.
- Market sharing: dividing sales territories or customer groups (common in the illegal drugs market).
- Collusive tendering (bid rigging): firms arrange bids so a chosen firm wins. School example: honest lowest bid 2 million euro; colluding bids A 5m, B 4m, C 3m - C wins and makes 1 million euro more.

OLIGOPOLY - CONCENTRATION, KINKED DEMAND AND EQUILIBRIUM
- Four-firm ratio over 50% suggests oligopoly. Car insurance example: sales 13, 10, 9, 8, 7, 2.5, 2, 1 million euro; total 52.5m; top four 40m = 76%. Implications: less choice, higher prices, easy collusion.
- Kinked demand curve (Figure 8.17, in words): demand curve with a kink at P1 (point B). Above P1 (AB) demand is relatively elastic - a price rise loses many sales. Below P1 (BC) it is relatively inelastic - rivals match cuts, little extra sold. Explains price rigidity.
- Equilibrium (Figure 8.18): kinked D/AR; MR has a vertical gap (discontinuous) below the kink; MC passes through the gap. Q1 where MR = MC; price P1; costs at C - if MC moves between D and E, P1 does not change. AR > AC, so supernormal profits.

REGULATION OF OLIGOPOLIES - THE CCPC
- Called 'antitrust legislation' in the US. Banking regulated by the Central Bank.
- CCPC: investigates anti-competitive behaviour and breaches of the Competition Act; prosecutes with the DPP (firms fined, individuals fined and jailed); assesses mergers and can block them (e.g. high HHI); enforces product safety; advocates competition; informs consumers of rights; regulates the grocery sector.
- Cartel Immunity Programme: immunity for the first firm or individual in a cartel to report it.

EVALUATION OF OLIGOPOLY
- Advantages: more choice than monopoly; innovation and variety (many health insurance policies); loyalty rewards; advertising creates jobs and media revenue, and sponsorship (Lidl and ladies' football); economies of scale may mean lower prices; stable prices help budgeting.
- Disadvantages: potential collusion; higher price and lower output than perfect competition; advertising costs passed on as higher prices; slow to pass on cost falls - fuel prices rise quickly but fall slowly; banks pass on ECB rate rises immediately but cuts slowly.

COMPARING THE FOUR MARKET STRUCTURES (TABLE 8.21)
- Number of firms: one / few large / dozens-hundreds / very many.
- Examples: Irish Rail / banking, insurance / fast food, coffee shops / agricultural produce.
- Barriers to entry: yes / yes / no / no.
- Product: no close substitute / differentiated / differentiated / homogenous.
- Demand curve: downward / kinked (MR discontinuous) / downward, slope depends on differentiation / horizontal, perfectly elastic (AR = MR).
- Concentration: high (HHI 10,000 pure monopoly) / high / low to medium / low (HHI near 1).
- Aims: profit max / may have other aims / profit max / profit max.
- Profits: SNP / SNP possible / SNP short run, normal long run / SNP short run, normal long run.

MONOPOLY VS PERFECT COMPETITION IN THE LONG RUN (FIGURE 8.19)
- Same AC and MC assumed. Draw the monopoly graph, then a horizontal D = AR = MR (PC) line tangent to the lowest point of AC.
- Quantity: monopoly QM lower; perfect competition QPC higher.
- Price: monopoly PM higher; perfect competition PPC lower.
- Efficiency: monopoly inefficient; perfect competition efficient (lowest AC).
- Profit: monopoly SNP (AR > AC); perfect competition normal profit (AR = AC).

rows.prompt: A firm is earning supernormal profit when:
rows.explanation: Supernormal (abnormal) profit is earned when revenue per unit exceeds cost per unit.

rows.prompt: How is the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) calculated?
options: Add the market shares of the four largest firms
Multiply the number of firms by the largest share
Divide total sales by the number of firms
Square each firm's market share and add the results
rows.explanation: The HHI is the sum of the squared percentage market shares.

rows.prompt: Four airlines have 40%, 42%, 8% and 10% of the market. What is the HHI?
The Irish CCPC regards a post-merger HHI above what value as highly concentrated?
rows.explanation: The CCPC sees over 1,000 as concentrated and over 2,000 as highly concentrated.

rows.prompt: In perfect competition, goods sold by different suppliers are:
rows.explanation: Identical products mean perfect substitutes are widely available.

rows.prompt: Why is a perfectly competitive firm called a price taker?
options: It sets the price for the whole market
It can set price or quantity but not both
It sells a tiny share of output so must accept the market price
It agrees prices with its rivals
rows.explanation: Price is set by the market and each firm must charge it.

rows.prompt: The demand curve facing an individual perfectly competitive firm is:
rows.explanation: Any price above the market price means demand falls to zero.

rows.prompt: In perfect competition, which is true?
rows.explanation: Each extra unit adds the price to revenue, and revenue per unit is the price.

rows.prompt: A perfectly competitive firm has AR 60 euro, AC 45 euro and sells 100 units. Supernormal profit is:
Why are supernormal profits eliminated in perfect competition in the long run?
options: The government taxes away the profits
Firms agree to cut their prices
Barriers to entry are put in place
New firms enter, increasing supply and lowering price
rows.explanation: Knowledge of profits and no barriers mean entry, pushing price down to minimum AC.

rows.prompt: Why does competitive advertising not occur in perfect competition?
options: Products are identical, so a firm would also advertise its rivals' goods
Buyers have no knowledge of prices
Firms earn too much profit to need it
rows.explanation: The firm would pay all the cost but all sellers would gain the sales.

rows.prompt: The short run supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm is the part of the MC curve above:
rows.explanation: In the short run the firm must at least cover its average variable costs.

rows.prompt: What is the source of a monopoly's power?
rows.explanation: Barriers prevent new firms from entering and competing.

rows.prompt: De Beers' control of diamond mines is an example of which barrier to entry?
rows.explanation: Controlling the mines meant no other firm could supply diamonds.

rows.prompt: Why does the monopolist's MR curve lie below its AR curve?
options: Its costs rise as output increases
To sell more it must cut the price on all units
The government sets a price ceiling
It faces a horizontal demand curve
rows.explanation: Lowering the price applies to every unit, not just the extra one.

rows.prompt: Price falls from 16 euro (3 units) to 14 euro (4 units). TR goes from 48 euro to 56 euro. MR of the 4th unit is:
rows.explanation: MR = change in TR = 56 - 48 = 8 euro.

rows.prompt: Why can a monopoly earn supernormal profit in the long run?
options: Barriers to entry stop new firms entering
It produces at the lowest point on AC
rows.explanation: Without new entrants, SNPs are not competed away.

rows.prompt: A monopolist has AR 20 euro, AC 10 euro and sells 8 units. Its supernormal profit is:
Removing laws that stop new firms entering a market, as happened in Irish electricity, is called:
rows.explanation: Deregulation removed barriers so firms like Energia and SSE Airtricity could enter.

rows.prompt: A hairdresser charges students and pensioners less than other customers. This is:
rows.explanation: Customers are grouped by price elasticity of demand.

rows.prompt: Which is a condition for price discrimination to work?
options: There must be no barriers to entry
All customers must have the same elasticity
Markets must be kept separate so goods cannot be resold
rows.explanation: Low-price buyers must not be able to resell to high-price buyers.

rows.prompt: Selling one bar for 1 euro or three bars for 2 euro is an example of:
rows.explanation: Second-degree gives discounts for bulk purchases.

rows.prompt: Which is a feature of monopolistic (imperfect) competition?
options: One seller with no close substitutes
Product differentiation with no barriers to entry
rows.explanation: Firms sell similar but not identical products and can enter freely.

rows.prompt: A firm that builds strong brand loyalty will have a demand curve that is:
rows.explanation: Loyal customers are less price sensitive, giving the firm more power over price.

rows.prompt: In long run equilibrium, a firm in monopolistic competition:
options: Earns supernormal profit and is efficient
Earns normal profit but is inefficient
Earns normal profit and is efficient
Earns supernormal profit and is inefficient
rows.explanation: AR = AC, but output is not at the lowest point of AC.

rows.prompt: Firms in an oligopoly are described as interdependent because they:
options: Take the likely reactions of rivals into account
Are owned by the same company
rows.explanation: Pricing decisions depend on how rivals are expected to respond.

rows.prompt: Price rigidity in oligopoly means that prices:
options: Fall to the lowest point on AC
Tend not to change even when costs change
rows.explanation: A rise loses sales and a cut starts a price war, so prices stay put.

rows.prompt: On the kinked demand curve, the section above the current price is:
options: Relatively inelastic, as rivals match a price rise
Relatively elastic, as rivals do not follow a price rise
Perfectly elastic, as the firm is a price taker
Perfectly inelastic, as demand never changes
rows.explanation: A price rise loses many sales to rivals who keep their prices.

rows.prompt: Existing firms cutting prices to deter a new airline from entering is called:
rows.explanation: Limit pricing makes entry unprofitable and is illegal.

rows.prompt: Firms A, B and C agree that C will win a school contract by bidding lowest. This is:
rows.explanation: Firms arrange their bids so the chosen bidder wins.

rows.prompt: Top four firms' sales are 40m euro out of total market sales of 52.5m euro. The four-firm ratio is about:
rows.explanation: 40 / 52.5 x 100 = 76% (rounded), suggesting oligopoly.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a high and a low market concentration, giving an example of each.
rows.model_answer: A highly concentrated market has a small number of large sellers that dominate, e.g. mobile phone networks or retail banks; this means less choice and higher prices. A market with low concentration has many smaller sellers, e.g. a fruit market or city restaurants; this generally means more choice and lower prices.

rows.prompt: State five characteristics of perfectly competitive markets.
rows.model_answer: Freedom of entry and exit for sellers. Homogenous (identical) goods with perfect substitutes. Many buyers who cannot influence price. A high degree of knowledge among buyers and sellers. Many sellers who are price takers, and firms aim to maximise profit (MR = MC).

rows.prompt: Describe in words the long run equilibrium diagram of a firm in perfect competition and state its four key features.
rows.model_answer: Price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal; a horizontal D/MR/AR line touches the lowest point of a U-shaped AC curve, and the MC curve passes through that same point E. The firm produces Q2 where MR = MC, charges the market price P2, is efficient because it produces at the lowest point of AC, and earns normal profit because AR = AC.

rows.prompt: Name and explain three barriers to entry.
rows.model_answer: Patents give the inventor the sole right to supply an invention for a period, e.g. new medicines. Economies of scale give an established firm a lower cost per unit than a new small entrant, e.g. a large airline on a route. A statutory monopoly is where a law gives one firm the only licence, e.g. Dublin Bus until 2017.

rows.prompt: Define price discrimination and state the conditions needed for it to work.
rows.model_answer: Price discrimination is charging different customers different prices for the same good or service where the difference is not due to cost differences. It needs some monopoly power, the ability to identify groups with different price elasticities, markets kept separate so the good cannot be resold, and consumer indifference among those paying more.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by product differentiation and give three methods firms use to achieve it.
rows.model_answer: Product differentiation means firms sell goods that are similar but not identical, so they are close but not perfect substitutes. Methods include branding and competitive advertising, distinctive packaging, product quality and innovation, loyalty cards and customer service.

rows.prompt: Distinguish between price rigidity and price constancy.
rows.model_answer: Price rigidity is when oligopoly firms keep prices unchanged even if costs change, because a price rise would lose sales to rivals and a price cut would start a price war. Price constancy is leaving price unchanged because changing it would cost more than the lost profit, e.g. reprinting menus or catalogues.

rows.prompt: Explain the term 'collusion' and give three examples of collusion.
rows.model_answer: Collusion is when competing firms agree not to compete in order to raise their profits at the expense of consumers, e.g. by forming a cartel; it is usually illegal. Examples are price fixing (BA and Virgin Atlantic fuel surcharges), market sharing (dividing sales territories), collusive tendering, price leadership and restricting output (OPEC).

rows.prompt: Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the equilibrium position of a firm operating as a monopoly. Refer to quantity, price, costs (efficiency) and profits. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Diagram (in words): price/costs on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal. A downward-sloping D/AR curve with a steeper MR curve below it; a U-shaped AC curve and a Nike-shaped MC curve that cuts MR from below at point E. From Q1 go up to the demand curve at X to find P1, and up to the AC curve at C to find C1. The rectangle P1C1CX is shaded as supernormal profit. Quantity: the firm produces Q1, the profit-maximising output where MR = MC and MC cuts MR from below. Price: P1 is the price it must charge to sell Q1, read off the demand curve. Costs: the cost per unit is C, which is not the lowest point on the AC curve, so the monopolist is inefficient and wasteful of resources. Profits: AR > AC at Q1, so supernormal profits are earned, in both the short run and the long run, because barriers to entry prevent new firms entering.
rows.marking_scheme: Diagram 8 marks: axes 1m, D/AR and MR diverging 2m, AC and MC 2m, equilibrium at MR = MC with P1 and C1 2m, SNP area 1m. Explanation: 4 points x 3 marks (quantity, price, efficiency, profits) = 12m. Total 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain, with the aid of diagrams, how a firm in a perfectly competitive market moves from short run to long run equilibrium. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: Short run diagram (in words): a horizontal D/MR/AR line at P1; a U-shaped AC and an MC curve cutting MR from below at E above Q1; AC at Q1 is at C, below P1; the area P1C1CE is supernormal profit. In the short run the firm produces Q1 where MR = MC, charges the market price P1, is inefficient (not at lowest AC) and earns supernormal profit as AR > AC. Movement to the long run: sellers have a high degree of knowledge of profits, and there are no barriers to entry, so new firms enter. Market supply shifts to the right and the market price falls from P(old) to P(new). As a price taker, the individual firm must accept the lower price, so its D/MR/AR line moves down. Long run diagram (in words): the new horizontal D/MR/AR line at P2 is tangent to the lowest point of the AC curve, and MC passes through that point E above Q2. In the long run the firm produces a lower quantity Q2 where MR = MC, charges a lower price P2, is efficient because it produces at the lowest point of AC, and earns only normal profit because AR = AC.
rows.marking_scheme: Short run diagram 5m; long run diagram 5m (or market diagram showing supply shift). Short run explanation 5m (output/price 2m, efficiency 1m, SNP 2m). Reasons for change: 2 points x 2.5m (knowledge of profits, no barriers to entry/supply shifts and price falls) = 5m. Long run explanation 5m (output/price 2m, efficient 1m, normal profit 2m). Total 25 marks.

rows.prompt: A country has five broadband suppliers with market shares: A 30%, B 45%, C 10%, D 10%, E 5%. Firms A and B plan to merge. (i) Calculate the HHI before the merger. (ii) Calculate the HHI after the merger. (iii) Would regulators approve the merger? Explain. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) Square each share and add: 30 squared = 900; 45 squared = 2,025; 10 squared = 100; 10 squared = 100; 5 squared = 25. HHI before = 3,150, which is already high market concentration (above 2,500). (ii) After merging A and B have 75%: 75 squared = 5,625; plus 100 + 100 + 25 = 225. HHI after = 5,850. (iii) Regulators would probably not approve. The HHI would rise sharply to 5,850, far above the CCPC's 2,000 threshold for a highly concentrated market and the European Commission's 2,000 level of concern. The merged firm would hold 75% of the market and dominate it, so it could abuse its position by charging higher prices, restricting output or giving poor service, which is not in the interest of consumers.
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 6 marks: method 2m + correct answer 4m. (ii) 6 marks: method 2m + correct answer 4m. (iii) 8 marks: decision 2m + 2 reasons x 3m referring to HHI values/thresholds and consumer harm.

rows.prompt: State and explain five features of oligopolistic markets. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: 1. High concentration ratio: a small number of large firms dominate, e.g. Vodafone, Three and Eir in Irish telecoms. 2. Interdependence: firms take rivals' likely reactions into account, especially on price, leading to price rigidity, e.g. similar mortgage rates. 3. Product differentiation: close but not perfect substitutes, with heavy advertising and sponsorship and brand loyalty, e.g. bank slogans. 4. Barriers to entry: economies of scale, high start-up costs, limit pricing, brand loyalty and brand proliferation (e.g. Coca-Cola's range) deter entrants. 5. Non-price competition: firms avoid price wars and compete through advertising, loyalty cards, special offers and quality of service. 6. Possible collusion: few firms make it easy to form cartels, fix prices or share markets. 7. Aims other than profit maximisation, e.g. becoming market leader as Revolut did with very low fees.
rows.marking_scheme: 5 features x 4 marks (2 marks statement + 2 marks explanation/example). Total 20 marks.

rows.prompt: With the aid of a single diagram, compare the long run equilibrium of a monopolist with that of a perfectly competitive firm with the same costs. Refer to output, price, efficiency and profit. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Diagram (in words): one set of AC and MC curves. The monopoly has a downward-sloping D = AR [M] curve with MR [M] below it; MC cuts MR [M] at output QM and the price PM is read off the demand curve. The perfectly competitive firm has a horizontal D = AR = MR [PC] line drawn tangent to the lowest point of AC, at price PPC and output QPC. Output: the monopolist produces a lower quantity QM, while the perfectly competitive firm produces a higher quantity QPC. Price: the monopolist charges the higher price PM; the perfectly competitive firm charges the lower price PPC. Efficiency: the monopolist is inefficient as QM is not produced at the lowest point of AC; the perfectly competitive firm is efficient as QPC is at the lowest point of AC. Profit: the monopolist earns supernormal profit as AR > AC; the perfectly competitive firm earns normal profit as AR = AC.
rows.marking_scheme: Diagram 8 marks: monopoly curves 3m, PC demand tangent to min AC 3m, labels QM, QPC, PM, PPC 2m. Comparison: 4 points x 3 marks (output, price, efficiency, profit). Total 20 marks.
